lead: Plot y against x and forget t for a moment. For an autonomous system x′ = F(x, y), y′ = G(x, y), time is hidden, so each solution is a curve in the xy-plane. Where both derivatives vanish the curve has nowhere to go: that is a critical point. Linearise there, read the two eigenvalues, and you know whether nearby motion falls in, spirals around, or runs away. Engineers use this to judge whether a power grid, a drone controller or a chemical reactor returns to steady state after a knock.
prereq: You need characteristic roots and eigenvalues from Chapter 2.1, and first-order separable equations from Unit 1.

sections.h3: An ODE system with no clock

blocks.text: An autonomous system has no t on the right-hand side: x′ = F(x, y), y′ = G(x, y). Here x and y are the dependent variables, often position and velocity, or two competing populations. The prime means d/dt, and F, G are smooth functions. Because t is absent, the point (x, y) alone fixes the velocity (F, G).

A solution is a pair (x(t), y(t)). Plot it in the xy-plane and drop the t labels; the curve is a trajectory. The xy-plane is the phase plane. Time still runs along the curve, and an arrow marks the direction as t increases, but the shape is fixed by the vector field.

A critical point (equilibrium point) is a point (x₀, y₀) with F(x₀, y₀) = 0 and G(x₀, y₀) = 0. A solution starting exactly there stays there forever. The real question is what a solution starting nearby does: return, circle, or escape.
Shift the origin to the critical point so it sits at (0, 0). Taylor expansion near it keeps only the linear terms:
x′ = a x + b y,   y′ = c x + d y
blocks.where: a = F<sub>x</sub>(x₀, y₀), b = F<sub>y</sub>(x₀, y₀), c = G<sub>x</sub>(x₀, y₀), d = G<sub>y</sub>(x₀, y₀); subscripts mean partial derivatives.

blocks.text: The matrix of these coefficients is the Jacobian:
J = [[a, b], [c, d]] = [[F<sub>x</sub>, F<sub>y</sub>], [G<sub>x</sub>, G<sub>y</sub>]] at (x₀, y₀)
blocks.where: J is evaluated at the critical point only; it changes from point to point.

blocks.text: Try (x, y) = (u₁, u₂)e^(λt). Substitution gives J u = λ u, so λ is an eigenvalue and u an eigenvector. The eigenvalues solve

blocks.where: τ = λ₁ + λ₂ = a + d = trace J; Δ = λ₁λ₂ = ad − bc = det J.

blocks.text: Two numbers, τ and Δ, carry the local picture. The sign of Δ says whether the eigenvalues have the same sign (Δ > 0) or opposite signs (Δ < 0). The sign of τ says whether they grow (τ > 0) or decay (τ < 0). The discriminant τ² − 4Δ says real (≥ 0) or complex (< 0). When an eigenvalue has zero real part, linearisation is inconclusive and higher-order terms decide.
Put the conditions together and five pictures appear.

Stable means nearby solutions stay near for all t ≥ 0. Asymptotically stable means they also tend to the critical point as t → ∞. A node and a spiral can be either; a saddle never is. A centre is stable but not asymptotically stable: its trajectories are closed curves traced forever.

For distinct real eigenvalues, eigenvectors give two directions. A saddle has one stable and one unstable direction; a node has two (or, in the repeated defective case, only one) stable/unstable eigendirections. When τ² = 4Δ and Δ > 0, proper versus improper depends on whether the eigenspace is two-dimensional or one-dimensional. A spiral has none: every direction eventually curls in or out.

figure.caption: Arrows on the vertical axis point into the critical point; arrows on the horizontal axis point away. One eigenvalue is negative, one positive — the signature of a saddle.

spec.aria: A phase portrait with a critical point at the centre, arrows on the vertical axis pointing in towards it and arrows on the horizontal axis pointing away from it.

examples.question: Find and classify the critical point of x′ = x, y′ = −2y. Solve the system directly and describe the trajectories.
steps: Write F(x, y) = x and G(x, y) = −2y. Set F = 0 and G = 0: x = 0 and −2y = 0, so y = 0. The only critical point is (0, 0).
Compute the partial derivatives: F<sub>x</sub> = 1, F<sub>y</sub> = 0, G<sub>x</sub> = 0, G<sub>y</sub> = −2. The Jacobian at (0, 0) is J = [[1, 0], [0, −2]].
J is diagonal, so its eigenvalues are the diagonal entries: λ₁ = 1 and λ₂ = −2.
τ = λ₁ + λ₂ = 1 + (−2) = −1. Δ = λ₁λ₂ = 1 × (−2) = −2. Check: trace J = 1 + (−2) = −1 and det J = (1)(−2) − (0)(0) = −2, which agree.
Δ = −2 < 0, so the eigenvalues have opposite signs. The critical point is a saddle. A saddle is unstable whatever the sign of τ.

Solve directly. x′ = x gives x = C₁e^t. y′ = −2y gives y = C₂e^(−2t). Eliminate t: x² = C₁²e^(2t), so x²y = C₁²C₂e^(2t)e^(−2t) = C₁²C₂, a constant. The trajectories are the curves x²y = k, running out along the x-axis and in along the y-axis.
examples.answer: The critical point (0, 0) is a saddle with τ = −1 and Δ = −2; it is unstable, and the trajectories are x²y = constant.
examples.check:
a, b, c, d = 1.0, 0.0, 0.0, -2.0
tau = a + d
Delta = a*d - b*c
disc = tau*tau - 4*Delta
lam1 = (tau + disc**0.5)/2
lam2 = (tau - disc**0.5)/2
print(lam1)
print(lam2)
print(tau)
print(Delta)

traps: A saddle is never stable, even though one eigenvalue is negative and one family of solutions does approach the origin.
When Δ = 0 or an eigenvalue has zero real part, the linear terms do not decide: neglected quadratic terms can turn a centre into a spiral. Check the nonlinear system.
τ and Δ are trace and determinant of the Jacobian at the critical point, not of some coefficient matrix evaluated elsewhere.
A stable node approaches straight in; a stable spiral curls in. The discriminant τ² − 4Δ separates them.
If t appears on the right-hand side, the system is not autonomous: the vector field changes with time and trajectories can cross.

quiz.q: Define an autonomous system and a critical point.
quiz.a: An autonomous system is x′ = F(x, y), y′ = G(x, y) with no explicit t on the right. A critical point (x₀, y₀) satisfies F(x₀, y₀) = 0 and G(x₀, y₀) = 0.

quiz.q: Why can two trajectories of an autonomous system not cross in the phase plane?
quiz.a: At any point (x, y) the vector field gives one velocity (F, G). If two trajectories crossed, that point would have two different velocity directions, violating uniqueness of solutions.

quiz.q: Classify the critical point at the origin of x′ = −x + y, y′ = −x − y.
quiz.a: J = [[−1, 1], [−1, −1]]. τ = −2, Δ = (−1)(−1) − (1)(−1) = 2. τ² − 4Δ = 4 − 8 = −4 < 0, so the eigenvalues are complex with negative real part: a stable spiral.

quiz.q: A system has τ = 0 and Δ = 4. What does linearisation predict, and why is the prediction not trustworthy?
quiz.a: λ = ±2i, so linearisation predicts a centre with closed curves. The real parts are zero, so the neglected nonlinear terms decide whether nearby solutions spiral in, spiral out or close; a Lyapunov function or higher-order analysis is needed.

quiz.q: Find and classify the critical points of the pendulum system x′ = y, y′ = −sin x at (0, 0) and (π, 0).
quiz.a: J = [[0, 1], [−cos x, 0]]. At (0, 0): τ = 0, Δ = 1, a centre (linear prediction). At (π, 0): τ = 0, Δ = −1, a saddle.

quiz.q: Both eigenvalues of a critical point are −3. Find τ and Δ, name the picture, and state the stability.
quiz.a: τ = −3 + (−3) = −6, Δ = (−3)(−3) = 9. τ² = 36 = 4Δ, so the roots are real and repeated: a stable node, asymptotically stable. Equal eigenvalues do not force an improper node; proper versus improper depends on whether the eigenspace is two-dimensional or one-dimensional.

beyond: Not for the exam. Lyapunov functions prove stability when eigenvalues are inconclusive, and the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem explains when closed orbits (limit cycles) can exist in the plane. Bifurcation theory studies how the picture changes as a parameter crosses a value; a stable spiral becoming a limit cycle is a Hopf bifurcation. Power-system swing stability, drone attitude control and chemical-reactor safety all start from this phase-plane reading. Search terms: Jacobian linearisation, Hartman–Grobman theorem, Lyapunov function, limit cycle, Hopf bifurcation.
